tip: English "should have" hides a detour in French: aurions dû is literally "would have had to." Past regret = conditional of devoir + infinitive.
Manquer flips the subject: lui manque means the country is missing TO him, so HE misses it. The thing missed is the subject; the person is lui, me, te.
French uses où (literally "where") for time too: le jour où = "the day when," never "the day where." Same with l'année où and le moment où.
Venir de + verb means "just did," not "come to": viennent d'emménager = "just moved in." A present-tense verb covers the recent past.
After avant de, French wants the infinitive, not the -ing form: avant de déménager = "before moving." Same pattern with sans and pour + infinitive.
en + the -ant form means "while/on doing": en partant = "as I was leaving." This is the one spot French uses this gerund shape.
Color words land after the noun in French: un chapeau rouge, not "un rouge chapeau." Most everyday adjectives follow the noun this way.
Information is plural in French: les informations... sont takes a plural verb, while English keeps "information is" singular and uncountable.
French drops "a" before a job after être: est pilote = "is a pilot," not "est un pilote." The article returns only once you describe the job.
Dont means "whose" here, and French keeps the article: dont la culture = "whose culture." You never drop the la the way English drops "the."
The si-half never takes the conditional: si tu avais fait (had done), then tu aurais compris (would have understood). Only the result half gets "would."
Two past tenses split the job: me préparais (imperfect) sets the ongoing scene, tu m'as envoyé (perfect) is the single action that cuts in.
After quand, French uses the future where English uses the present perfect: nous aurons déjeuné = "when we've had lunch." No present tense here.
quoique (one word) = "although"; quoi que (two words) = "whatever." Here quoiqu'elle eût means "although she had," and the verb turns subjunctive.
Sans que forces the subjunctive: sans qu'elle le sût = "without her knowing." Trigger words like sans que and avant que always pull this mood.
Nul ne is a bookish "no one," working like personne ne: Nul ne croyait = "no one believed." The ne stays and there's no pas with these negatives.
